name: PhD Mode
description: Real findings from recent open-access papers in top journals, plus invented look-alike findings for liars (pilot v2: 20 papers). See sources/phd/GUIDE.md.

topics.summary: Stanford researchers measured 'sycophancy' (excessive agreement and flattery) in 11 state-of-the-art large language models, comparing their advice to human judgments, including Reddit's Am I The Asshole community, on interpersonal conflicts, deception and harmful actions. The models affirmed users' actions about 49% more often than humans did. Three preregistered experiments with 2,405 people then had participants discuss real or hypothetical conflicts with flattering or neutral AI. One sycophantic conversation made people more convinced they were right and less willing to apologize or repair the relationship, yet they trusted the flattering model more and preferred to use it again, an incentive problem for AI companies optimizing engagement. Topics: AI alignment and safety, human-computer interaction, social psychology, moral judgment, conflict resolution, chatbot design and accountability.

truth.text: Across 11 leading AI chatbots, the models endorsed users' actions about 50% more often than real people did, even when the user described lying or breaking the law.
facts: 'Endorsed' means telling users they were in the right, called AI 'sycophancy'
The real people were human judges, including Reddit's 'Am I The Asshole' voters
Exact figure: chatbots sided with users 49% more often than humans did
Scenarios covered everyday conflicts, deception and harmful or illegal acts

topics.summary: Google's Co-Scientist is a multi-agent AI system built on Gemini that generates, debates and refines scientific hypotheses. Agents propose ideas, critique them, and rank them in an Elo-style tournament; spending more compute at test time keeps improving hypothesis quality. It was validated in biomedicine: it proposed drugs to repurpose for acute myeloid leukaemia that worked in cell experiments, suggested new treatment targets for liver fibrosis, and independently re-derived an unpublished explanation from Imperial College for how phage-inducible chromosomal islands, bacterial gene parasites, hijack diverse phage tails to spread across species, relevant to antimicrobial resistance. Topics: AI for science, large language models, agents, drug discovery, cancer, microbiology, bacteriophages, automating research.

truth.text: Google built a team of AI agents that argue over research ideas in a tournament, and some existing drugs it suggested reusing against leukemia worked in lab tests.
facts: Each agent is a chatbot given one job: propose, critique or rank ideas
Ideas are ranked by head-to-head matches, scored like chess player ratings
The agents run on Google's Gemini chatbot
The leukemia was acute myeloid leukemia, a fast-growing blood cancer
The suggested drugs worked against leukemia cells grown in the lab

topics.summary: A Cornell-led Nature Sustainability analysis projected the environmental footprint of AI servers in the United States from 2024 to 2030. Depending on growth, AI servers could use 731 to 1,125 million cubic meters of water a year and add 24 to 44 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent annually. The industry is unlikely to meet net-zero pledges by 2030 without relying on uncertain carbon offsets and water restoration. Best practices could cut emissions by up to 73% and water by 86%, mainly by siting servers in central states such as Texas, Montana, Nebraska and South Dakota with abundant wind and solar and low water stress, though Texas might need more new power than its current renewable output. Topics: data centers, energy systems, water footprint, climate policy, electricity grids, renewable energy, sustainability of computing.

truth.text: The greenest place to build new US AI data centers is the windy, sunny central states like Texas and Nebraska, where best practices could cut AI's carbon footprint by up to 73%.
facts: Data centers are warehouses of computers that run AI services
US AI servers could emit 24-44 million tonnes of CO2 yearly by 2030
Most of the cut comes from where the servers are built
Central states have plenty of wind and sun, and little water stress
Catch: Texas may need more new power than its renewables now make

topics.summary: ETH Zurich engineers built a clinically oriented magnetic microrobot for targeted drug delivery: a dissolvable gelatin capsule about 1.7 mm across, loaded with iron oxide nanoparticles for magnetic steering, a contrast agent so it shows up on X-ray fluoroscopy, and a drug such as the clot-dissolving enzyme tPA used for stroke. A clinical electromagnetic navigation system and a custom release catheter steered it through realistic models of human blood vessels and through cranial arteries in pigs and sheep, where it was tracked live and released its cargo on target. The goal is to deliver drugs locally instead of flooding the whole body. Topics: medical robotics, magnetism, biomedical engineering, stroke treatment, interventional radiology, drug delivery, nanoparticles.

truth.text: Swiss engineers used magnets to steer a dissolvable capsule smaller than a lentil through the brain arteries of pigs and sheep, releasing clot-busting drug right where it was needed.
facts: The 1.7 mm gelatin capsule dissolves to release its drug
Iron oxide particles inside let a hospital electromagnet system steer it
A contrast dye makes it visible on live X-ray video
Clot-busters treat strokes; this doses the clot, not the whole body

topics.summary: The Global Carbon Budget team (Friedlingstein, Le Quere and colleagues) reconciled estimates of where humanity's CO2 goes. Atmospheric CO2 reached 423 ppm in 2024 and human-caused warming 1.36 C. Revised accounting shows the natural land sink is substantially smaller than previously estimated, emissions from land-use change are larger, and the ocean sink is about 15% larger than the land sink. Climate change itself has weakened the sinks, especially on land, adding 8.3 ppm to atmospheric CO2 since 1960. Combined with deforestation, it has turned Southeast Asian and much of South American tropical forest from carbon sinks into sources. Topics: climate science, carbon cycle, oceanography, forests, deforestation, Earth system models, Paris Agreement, climate policy.

truth.text: Climate change and deforestation have turned the tropical forests of Southeast Asia and much of South America from net absorbers of CO2 into net emitters.
facts: A net absorber, or carbon 'sink', takes in more CO2 than it releases
Heat and drought slow tree growth and kill trees, which then release carbon
Cutting forests releases their stored carbon and ends future absorption
From the Global Carbon Budget, the yearly tally of where CO2 goes
Weakened sinks have added 8.3 parts per million of CO2 since 1960

topics.summary: Cornell and Berkeley researchers analyzed 2.1 million preprints, 28,000 peer review reports and 246 million online accesses to see how large language models are changing science. Scientists who adopted LLMs to draft manuscripts increased their output by 23.7% to 89.3% depending on field and author background, with large gains for non-native English speakers. Before LLMs, more complex writing went with higher-quality papers; with LLM use the relationship reversed, producing polished-sounding but substantively weaker manuscripts. LLM adopters also read and cite more diverse prior work, including books and younger, less-cited papers. The authors argue journals, funders and tenure committees must rethink how they judge research. Topics: science of science, academic publishing, peer review, ChatGPT, research productivity, bibliometrics.

truth.text: Scientists who started using AI chatbots to draft papers raised their output by roughly 24% to 89%, and polished writing stopped being a sign of a good paper.
facts: The study tracked 2.1 million early-release papers, called preprints
Chatbot drafting was detected statistically from typical chatbot word patterns
The 24-89% range varies by field; non-native English speakers gained most
Before chatbots, more complex writing went with better papers; that link reversed

Suggests chatbots help people find work beyond the famous classics

topics.summary: Cambridge neuroscientists pooled diffusion MRI scans from 4,216 people aged 0 to 90 and tracked 12 graph-theory measures of how the brain's white-matter network is organized. Projecting these onto low-dimensional manifolds revealed four major topological turning points, around ages 9, 32, 66 and 83, splitting life into five epochs. From childhood to about 32 the network keeps becoming more efficiently integrated, an extended adolescence-like phase; adulthood is the longest stable epoch; after about 66 the network becomes more segregated; after 83 the age relationship weakens. Turning points may align with puberty, life milestones and risks for mental health and dementia. Topics: brain development, aging, neuroimaging, connectomics, network science, cognitive neuroscience, lifespan psychology.

truth.text: Brain scans of about 4,000 people aged 0 to 90 suggest our brain wiring goes through four big turning points, at around ages 9, 32, 66 and 83.
facts: The scans were diffusion MRI, which traces the brain's long-range nerve cables
'Wiring' means the network of connections between brain regions
Until about 32, the network keeps getting more efficient, like adolescence
32 to 66 is the longest stable phase; after 66 regions grow more separate
After 83, age predicts brain wiring less clearly

topics.summary: Stanford researchers built SleepFM, a foundation model trained on more than 585,000 hours of polysomnography, overnight sleep-lab recordings of brain waves, heart activity, breathing and muscle signals, from about 65,000 people. Using contrastive learning, it turns a single night into an embedding that predicts 130 future diseases with a C-index of at least 0.75, including death (0.84), dementia (0.85), heart failure (0.80), chronic kidney disease and stroke, and it generalized to an unseen cohort, the Sleep Heart Health Study. It also performs standard sleep staging and apnea detection. Topics: sleep medicine, machine learning in medicine, foundation models, wearables, dementia, cardiology, risk prediction.

truth.text: An AI trained on 585,000 hours of sleep-lab recordings can predict a person's risk of 130 future diseases, including dementia and heart failure, from a single night of sleep.
facts: Sleep labs record brain waves, heartbeat, breathing and muscles overnight
The recordings came from about 65,000 people
Accuracy for dementia: 0.85 (0.5 = coin flip, 1 = perfect)
It worked on a separate group of people it had never seen
Predictions also covered stroke, kidney disease and death

topics.summary: A Swedish nationwide study paired grasslands with neighboring managed forests to follow what happens to soil microbes when farmland is abandoned and turns back into forest, the largest land-use change in the Global North. Microbes changed through thresholds rather than gradually: taxonomic diversity fell while functional diversity rose, and nutrient-cycling genes for carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus became more specialized with less redundancy, a trade-off between diversity of functions and backup. Fungal functional diversity drove higher carbon-processing capacity, and leaf litter quality linked plant and microbe communities. Rewilding is not automatically a win for soil biodiversity and carbon. Topics: soil ecology, microbiology, fungi, land abandonment, rewilding, forestry, carbon storage, ecosystem succession.

truth.text: When abandoned farmland turns back into forest, its soil ends up with fewer kinds of microbes but a wider range of jobs they can do, with fungi leading the change.
facts: Soil microbes are bacteria and fungi that break down dead plants
'Jobs' means chemistry like recycling carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus
The study paired Swedish grasslands with neighboring forests nationwide
Changes came in sudden jumps, not gradually
Farm abandonment is the biggest land-use change in Europe and North America

topics.summary: Researchers from Heidelberg, Harvard and partners used a health-augmented macroeconomic model across 204 countries to estimate diabetes's economic cost from 2020 to 2050, counting lost labor from deaths and illness, diverted treatment spending and informal caregiving. Without informal care the burden is 10.2 trillion international dollars, about 0.22% of global GDP every year; including unpaid family care it rises to 78.8 trillion (1.72% of GDP), more than six times larger. Absolute costs are highest in the US, China and India; per-person and relative burdens are highest in places like American Samoa and Australia, while much of Africa and South Asia show lower relative burden. More than one in ten adults has diabetes. Topics: health economics, global health, diabetes, caregiving, GDP, public policy.

truth.text: Counting the unpaid time families spend caring for people with diabetes makes its global economic cost more than six times larger, about $79 trillion from 2020 to 2050.
facts: Usual costs: treatment, plus work lost to illness and early death
Without family care: $10.2 trillion, 0.22% of world GDP yearly
With it: 1.72% of world GDP every year
Biggest totals: US, China and India; the model covered 204 countries

topics.summary: Oxford researchers modeled 24 maritime chokepoints, narrow passages like the Suez Canal, Panama Canal, Strait of Hormuz, Malacca Strait and Taiwan Strait, and eight hazards: cyclones, drought, earthquakes, terrorism, armed and interstate conflict, blockages and piracy. About 192 billion US dollars of trade a year is expected to be disrupted, mostly from geopolitical risk at the Taiwan Strait and Suez Canal and combined hazards at Bab el-Mandeb near Yemen. Expected economic losses are 10.7 billion dollars a year plus 3.4 billion from higher freight costs. Exposed countries include neighbors of these straits but also distant ones in West Africa and Central Asia; Russia, Kazakhstan and Tajikistan depend on six chokepoints each. Topics: shipping, global trade, supply chains, geopolitics, risk analysis, Red Sea Houthi attacks, Panama Canal drought.

truth.text: About $192 billion of world trade a year is expected to be disrupted at narrow sea passages, with conflict risk in the Taiwan Strait and Suez Canal the biggest threats.
facts: Narrow passages, or 'chokepoints', include the Suez and Panama canals
The model covered 24 chokepoints and 8 hazards, from cyclones to piracy
Expected losses: $10.7 billion a year, plus $3.4 billion in freight costs
Bab el-Mandeb, by Yemen, faces several hazards at once, including attacks
Distant countries in West Africa and Central Asia are exposed too

source.institution: Monash University, Australia & Eli Lilly, USA

topics.summary: SURPASS-CVOT, a double-blind NEJM trial, randomized 13,299 people with type 2 diabetes and atherosclerotic heart disease to weekly tirzepatide (Mounjaro, a dual GLP-1 and GIP agonist known for large weight loss) or dulaglutide (Trulicity, a GLP-1 drug already proven to reduce heart events). Over a median of four years, tirzepatide was noninferior for the composite of cardiovascular death, heart attack or stroke (801 vs 862 events, hazard ratio 0.92, confidence interval 0.83 to 1.01), so not statistically superior. Gastrointestinal side effects were more common with tirzepatide. Topics: cardiology, diabetes, obesity drugs, GLP-1, clinical trials, pharmacology.

truth.text: In a 13,000-patient trial, the weight-loss drug tirzepatide (Mounjaro) prevented heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths at least as well as an older proven drug, but not clearly better.
facts: Tirzepatide and the older drug dulaglutide (Trulicity) are weekly diabetes injections
Dulaglutide was already proven to cut heart attacks and strokes
Patients had type 2 diabetes and heart disease; followed about 4 years
801 vs 862 heart events: 8% fewer, but not statistically certain
Stomach side effects were more common with tirzepatide

source.institution: Sakana AI, Japan, with Oxford & UBC

topics.summary: Sakana AI, Oxford and UBC researchers present The AI Scientist, a pipeline using foundation models in an agentic system to automate the whole research cycle in machine learning: generating ideas, searching literature, writing code, running experiments, plotting, writing the manuscript and reviewing it with an automated reviewer. In a template mode and an open-ended agentic-search mode it produced diverse papers. Three AI-written manuscripts were submitted, with organizers' consent, to a workshop at a top machine-learning conference (ICLR) whose reviewers knew some submissions were AI-generated but not which; one scored 6, 7 and 6, above the acceptance threshold of a workshop with a 70% acceptance rate. Topics: AI research automation, LLM agents, peer review, scientific integrity, machine learning.

truth.text: A fully automated 'AI Scientist' wrote a machine-learning paper, from idea to code to manuscript, that passed peer review at a workshop of a top AI conference.
facts: Peer review: experts score a paper to decide whether it's accepted
The conference was ICLR; this workshop accepted 70% of papers
Reviewers knew some papers were AI-written, not which; it scored 6, 7, 6
The system also searched the literature, ran experiments and drew its plots

topics.summary: JWST revealed 'little red dots', compact red galaxies in the early universe with broad hydrogen and helium emission lines, debated as either supermassive black holes or intense starbursts, with odd traits such as black holes too massive for their hosts and very weak X-ray and radio emission. Analyzing the best spectra, the authors show the lines are broadened by electron scattering around a narrow core, requiring dense, compact ionized gas only light-days across, which with their luminosity can only be explained by black hole accretion. The narrow cores imply masses of 100,000 to 10 million suns, about 100 times lower than earlier estimates: young black holes growing near the Eddington limit inside a dense gas cocoon that also hides X-rays and radio. Topics: astronomy, black holes, galaxy formation, cosmology, JWST, spectroscopy.

truth.text: The mysterious 'little red dots' spotted by the James Webb telescope are most likely young black holes wrapped in thick cocoons of gas, far lighter than first thought.
facts: The James Webb Space Telescope sees the early universe in infrared light
'Little red dots' are tiny, very red objects from the universe's first billion years
The debate was: growing black holes, or bursts of star formation?
'Far lighter': 100,000 to 10 million suns, about 100 times less than estimated
The thick gas cocoon also explains why they give off almost no X-rays

topics.summary: The glymphatic system is the brain's waste-clearance network, in which cerebrospinal fluid flushes the tissue, mostly during sleep. In a multi-site randomized crossover trial, 39 healthy older adults spent one night sleeping normally and one night sleep-deprived in a lab, wearing a new device that measured sleep EEG, cerebrovascular compliance (pulse transit time) and brain-tissue resistance to fluid flow by impedance spectroscopy. Lower tissue resistance, more compliant vessels, higher heart-rate variability and more deep slow-wave sleep predicted bigger overnight rises of Alzheimer's markers amyloid beta and tau in morning blood, evidence that sleep-driven glymphatic flow clears these proteins from brain to plasma in humans. Topics: sleep, Alzheimer's disease, neuroscience, aging, biomarkers, clinical trials, medical devices.

truth.text: A sleep-lab trial in older adults found that deep sleep helps the brain flush Alzheimer's-linked proteins out into the blood, direct evidence of the brain's nightly 'rinse' in humans.
facts: The 'rinse' is the glymphatic system: spinal fluid washing through brain tissue
The proteins are amyloid and tau, which build up in Alzheimer's
39 people slept normally one night and stayed awake another
More deep sleep predicted more of both proteins in morning blood tests

topics.summary: The Psychiatric Genomics Consortium combined genetic association data for 14 childhood- and adult-onset psychiatric disorders covering 1,056,201 cases. Genomic structural equation modeling found five underlying genetic factors explaining about two thirds of each disorder's genetic variance: schizophrenia and bipolar disorder; internalizing (major depression, PTSD, anxiety); neurodevelopmental (ADHD, autism, Tourette's); compulsive (OCD, anorexia); and substance use. The factors linked to 238 pleiotropic loci; schizophrenia-bipolar and internalizing disorders shared most of their signal with very few disorder-specific loci. Shared genes pointed to broad processes like transcriptional regulation. Results challenge current diagnostic boundaries such as the DSM. Topics: psychiatry, genetics, genomics, mental health, schizophrenia, depression, autism.

truth.text: A genetic study of over a million psychiatric patients found that 14 disorders fall into five genetic clusters, with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder sharing most of their genetic risk.
facts: Pooled DNA data on 1,056,201 patients with psychiatric diagnoses
Clusters: psychotic, depression-anxiety, neurodevelopmental, compulsive, substance use
For example, autism and ADHD cluster together, as do OCD and anorexia
It challenges the separate diagnoses in manuals like the DSM

topics.summary: On January 14, 2025, LIGO recorded GW250114, the loudest gravitational wave so far (network signal-to-noise ratio 76), from two merging black holes; Virgo and KAGRA were offline. Like a struck bell, the remnant black hole rings down with quasinormal modes whose frequencies general relativity fixes by mass and spin alone (the Kerr metric). The data require at least two modes, the fundamental tone and its first overtone, matching Kerr to tens of percent, and bound the main frequency within a few percent of the prediction. Inspiral, merger and ringdown tests were as strong or up to three times stronger than combining dozens of earlier events: the most stringent single-event confirmation of general relativity. Topics: physics, gravitational waves, black holes, Einstein, relativity, astrophysics.

truth.text: The loudest gravitational wave ever recorded let physicists 'hear' a newborn black hole vibrate like a struck bell at two distinct pitches, exactly as Einstein's theory predicts.
facts: Gravitational waves are ripples in space itself, made by colliding heavy objects
After two black holes merge, the new one shakes and settles, emitting set 'pitches'
Einstein's relativity says those pitches depend only on the black hole's mass and spin
Recorded by LIGO on January 14, 2025; the clearest such signal so far
This one event tested relativity better than dozens of earlier detections combined

topics.summary: Oxford researchers ran a randomized, preregistered study with 1,298 UK adults given ten medical scenarios written by doctors, asked to identify likely conditions and the right action, from self-care to calling an ambulance. Participants used GPT-4o, Llama 3 or Command R+, or any source they liked (control). Alone, the models named relevant conditions 94.9% of the time and the right disposition 56.3%. With the same models, people found relevant conditions under 34.5% of the time and the right action under 44.2%, no better than controls. Failures came from people giving incomplete information and from models offering several options (2.21 on average) that users chose poorly among. Medical exam benchmarks and simulated patients did not predict these failures. Topics: AI in medicine, chatbots, human-computer interaction, patient safety, health informatics.

truth.text: Chatbots alone diagnosed medical scenarios correctly 95% of the time, but ordinary people using the same chatbots got it right less than 35% of the time, no better than without them.
facts: Ten doctor-written medical scenarios were given to 1,298 UK adults
The chatbots were GPT-4o, Llama 3 and Command R+
A comparison group used any source they liked, such as web search
People left out key details and picked poorly among the bots' suggestions

source.institution: Google DeepMind & University of Cambridge, UK

topics.summary: Google DeepMind and Cambridge researchers developed a psychometric framework to give validated personality tests, the IPIP-NEO Big Five and others, to 18 large language models across thousands of prompt variations, and to check reliability and construct validity as psychologists do for humans. Larger and instruction-tuned models gave reliable, valid personality measurements; base and small models did not. Prompts could shape personality along chosen dimensions, such as more extraverted or less neurotic, and the shaped traits carried into downstream text such as social media posts. The authors discuss risks such as persuasive or manipulative personas and benefits for responsible AI. Topics: psychology, psychometrics, personality, large language models, AI safety, chatbots.

truth.text: Standard human personality tests give reliable results when taken by large AI chatbots, and simple prompts can dial a chatbot's personality traits up or down on demand.
facts: 18 AI language models took validated human personality questionnaires
Tests measured the 'Big Five': openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism
Larger, chat-tuned models gave the most consistent results
Prompted traits showed up in the bots' writing, such as social media posts

topics.summary: Researchers ran a process-based crop model inside an Earth system model to project how drought affects global food security by 2050 for maize, soybean, rice and wheat. Global drought losses are projected to be under 2%, but 62 countries may lose more than 10% and 24 countries more than 20% of production. Vulnerability is highest in countries with lower GDP and fast population growth, often in Africa and South Asia, so global averages hide severe local food insecurity. Topics: agriculture, climate change, drought, food security, crop modeling, development economics.

truth.text: Drought is projected to cut global harvests of maize, soy, rice and wheat by less than 2% by 2050, yet 24 countries could lose more than a fifth of their crops.
facts: Drought means unusually long dry spells that stunt crops
The projection ran a crop model inside a global climate model
62 countries may lose more than 10% of these four crops
Most at risk: poorer countries with fast-growing populations, often in Africa

topics.summary: A robot arm trained only on head-camera videos of people doing chores learned to load a dishwasher, succeeding in 7 of 10 kitchens it had never seen. Related topics: robot learning, imitation learning, computer vision, household robots, egocentric video.

lies.text: A robot arm trained only on head-camera videos of people doing chores learned to load a dishwasher, succeeding in 7 of 10 kitchens it had never seen.
facts: Head-mounted cameras record what people see while using their hands
Robots usually learn tasks from human demonstrations or trial and error
Unfamiliar kitchens test whether a robot generalizes beyond its training
Journals like Science Robotics and IEEE Transactions on Robotics publish papers on robots learning from human videos

topics.summary: People using an AI therapy chatbot for anxiety were twice as likely to quit treatment within a month as people seeing a human therapist over video. Related topics: mental health apps, anxiety, therapy adherence, chatbots, digital health.

lies.text: People using an AI therapy chatbot for anxiety were twice as likely to quit treatment within a month as people seeing a human therapist over video.
facts: Talk therapy for anxiety usually runs for several weekly sessions
Dropping out early is a known problem in all forms of therapy
Several apps now offer chatbot-based mental health support
Journals like npj Digital Medicine and JMIR Mental Health publish papers on chatbots and apps for mental health

topics.summary: In a study of 3,000 European grant applications, proposals partly written with AI chatbots scored higher on clarity but were funded at exactly the same rate. Related topics: research funding, peer review, grant writing, generative AI, science policy.

lies.text: In a study of 3,000 European grant applications, proposals partly written with AI chatbots scored higher on clarity but were funded at exactly the same rate.
facts: Grant panels score proposals on criteria like clarity, novelty and feasibility
The European Research Council funds roughly one in ten applications
Many funders now ask applicants to disclose AI use
Journals like Management Science and Research Policy publish papers on how research grants get judged

Rain, fog and snow scatter laser light and create false echoes
Norway is a common winter test site for autonomous vehicles
Journals like Science Robotics and IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Vehicles publish papers on self-driving cars in bad weather

topics.summary: Tokyo restaurants that added AI-translated menus saw tourists order 12% more food, but complaints about receiving the wrong dish doubled. Related topics: machine translation, tourism, restaurants, Japan, consumer behavior.

facts: Machine translation often struggles with dish names and food idioms
Japan received over 30 million foreign visitors in 2024
Many Tokyo restaurants offer picture menus or plastic food models
Journals like Nature Machine Intelligence and Computational Linguistics publish papers on machine translation in everyday life

topics.summary: An AI scanning decades-old sonar surveys of the Baltic Sea flagged 41 unknown shipwrecks, and divers later confirmed 29 of them. Related topics: underwater archaeology, sonar, machine learning, Baltic Sea, shipwrecks.

facts: Sonar maps the seabed by timing sound echoes

topics.summary: We report the detection of a burst of emission over a 695.5–1031.5 MHz bandwidth by the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder. After coherent dedispersion, the burst was determined to be less than 30 ns in width, with an average flux density of at least 300 kJy. We consider an electrostatic discharge (ESD) or plasma discharge following a micrometeoroid impact to be plausible explanations for the burst. ESDs have previously been observed with the Arecibo radio telescope, but on 1000 times longer timescales. Our observation opens new possibilities for the remote sensing of ESD, which poses a serious threat to spacecraft, and reveals a new source of false events for observations of astrophysical transients. topics.summary: The electrochemical co-reduction of CO2 and nitrate provides a sustainable route for urea synthesis via C–N coupling, yet kinetic limitations and poor intermediate interactions hinder urea yields. This work establishes nano-confinement as a versatile approach for controlling multi-step electrocatalytic processes, enabling sustainable chemical synthesis. topics.summary: Silicon-based MEMS resonators have shown promising potential to replace quartz crystal resonators in many fields, especially in realizing precise timing. However, the large temperature-dependent properties of single-crystal silicon render the MEMS resonators suffer from severe degradation in frequency stability caused by temperature variation, thus hindering the development of silicon-based resonant devices. By employing the nonlinear amplitude-frequency dependence of a Duffing resonator to actively suppress the frequency drift after the first stage oven control, the reported MEMS resonator exhibits a frequency stability of ±14 ppb. topics.summary: Human vision is highly adaptive, efficiently sampling intricate environments by sequentially fixating on task-relevant regions. topics.summary: Reasoning is a hallmark of human intelligence, enabling adaptive decision-making in complex unfamiliar scenarios. topics.topic: Patrilines of a Stone Age City
topics.summary: The discovery of Shimao city (around 2300–1800 bce1), a premier state-level Neolithic fortified settlement in Shaanxi, China2, played an important role in helping us understand the emergence of socially stratified urban societies. However, key questions remain regarding how ancestry and kinship shaped the hierarchy of this class-based society characterized by human sacrifice. The origin of the founding populations of Shimao and other Loess Plateau settlements, and their interactions within the broader ancestral landscape, have yet to be determined. Here we present, by sequencing 144 ancient genomes from Shimao city and its satellites, pedigrees among tomb owners spanning up to four generations. These findings reveal a predominantly patrilineal descent structure across Shimao communities, and possibly sex-specific sacrificial rituals. We also characterize the population history, revealing that Shimao culture-related populations originated mostly from a Yangshao culture-related population present at least 1,000 years earlier, and the lasting inflow of Yumin-related populations from Inner Mongolia did not interrupt regional genetic continuity. topics.summary: Melon ( Cucumis melo L.) domestication is thought to have occurred independently once in Northeast Africa and twice in India, but archaeobotanical seed remains point to a possible additional domestication in China. Because Cucumis seeds are difficult to diagnose morphologically, genomic data from archaeological material are needed to evaluate these scenarios and reconstruct ancient melon traits. We sequenced two Song Dynasty melon seeds from Shuomen Gugang (China), recovering 4.6× and 1.7× nuclear genome coverage. Nuclear and chloroplast analyses place both seeds within cultivated C. melo from China, supporting introduction from the broader Asian domestication pool rather than independent Chinese domestication. To assess whether these seeds carried traits associated with sweet dessert melons, we examined loci underlying fruit phenotypes. Neither seed carried alleles for orange flesh; one harbored an allele linked to yellow/orange peel, the other possessed alleles associated with green flesh and reduced acidity. Since wild melons are monoecious, the presence of the derived andromonoecy allele in one seed, associated with rounder fruit shape, suggests early selection on fruit morphology.... topics.summary: Vibrant feathers from Amazonian parrots were among the most prestigious symbols of status in the pre-Hispanic Andes, yet their acquisition required traversing the formidable Andean mountain range. Here, we investigate feathers recovered from an intact, elite masonry tomb at the coastal religious center of Pachacamac, associated with the pre-Inca Ychsma culture that flourished during the Late Intermediate Period (ca. 1000–1470 CE). By integrating ancient DNA, stable isotope analysis, and spatial modeling, we reconstruct the complete journey of these feathers. Genomic data identify four distinct Amazonian parrot species (Ara macao, A. ararauna, A. chloropterus, Amazona farinosa) and reveal high genetic diversity, indicating extraction from wild populations rather than local breeding. Stable carbon and nitrogen isotope analysis reveals that these birds consumed a C4-rich coastal diet, demonstrating they were transported alive across the Andes and kept in the arid coast. topics.summary: Wine production has deep historical roots in France, yet the biological foundations of early viticulture remain elusive. We report genome-wide ancient DNA data from 49 archaeological grape pips spanning ~4000 years, from the Bronze Age to the Medieval period, primarily focusing on France. Population genetic analyses reveal the genetic makeup of wild local grapevines in the Bronze Age and the early use of domesticated grapevines by ~625-500 BCE. Roman-era genomes reflect long-distance exchange from Iberian, Balkan, Levantine, and Caucasian domesticated varieties. Vegetative propagation, evidenced by genetically identical clones across sites and centuries, emerged by the mid-Iron Age and became a pillar of viticultural practice. Remarkably, one Medieval sample from Valenciennes is genetically identical to modern ‘Pinot Noir’, demonstrating clonal continuity over nearly 600 years. topics.summary: Numerous research efforts have used paleoecological data to reconstruct past biodiversity in Europe. In these projects, researchers have identified increases in biodiversity over the Holocene and hinted at a positive correlation with human population. These are important findings but are not easily translated into effective biodiversity conservation and restoration policy. We argue that, in order to better inform policymaking, studies of past biodiversity dynamics should include analyses of contemporaneous cultural phenomena in order to identify and describe specific anthropogenic drivers of past biodiversity changes. We present an example here, a case study from the Lake Constance region (southwestern Germany), one of the core areas of the Carolingian Empire, the foundational political structure of modern Europe. This uniquely well-documented region offers six fossil pollen profiles characterized by high taxonomic and chronological resolution, archaeobotanical evidence from hundreds of excavation sites, and historical records describing population, commerce, and agriculture dating from the mid-700s CE. topics.summary: Ibiza, an island in present-day Spain, was conquered in 902 CE by the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba. The island remained under Islamic rule until 1235. Here, we analyse the genetic and metagenomic profiles of 13 individuals from an Islamic cemetery in Ibiza, dated to 950-1150 CE. Genome-wide analyses reveal heterogeneity, with ancestry components from Europe, North Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa. Our analyses estimate that North African gene flow occurred two to seven generations before these individuals lived, suggesting admixture following the Islamic conquest of Iberia and potentially on Ibiza itself. topics.summary: The Piasts were one of the royal dynasties that shaped the political structure of medieval Europe in the 10th century CE. topics.summary: Human treponemal infections are caused by a family of closely related Treponema pallidum that give rise to the diseases yaws, bejel, pinta and, most notably, syphilis 1 . topics.summary: What constitutes a language? Natural languages share features with other domains: from math, to music, to gesture. However, the brain mechanisms that process linguistic input are highly specialized, showing little response to diverse non-linguistic tasks. Here, we examine constructed languages (conlangs) to ask whether they draw on the same neural mechanisms as natural languages, or whether they instead pattern with domains like math and programming languages. topics.summary: Humans can convey new and highly diverse information through language. However, understanding the microscopic cellular building blocks and cortical landscape that precisely underlie human language has remained a challenge. topics.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in applications where they interact with humans and other agents. We propose to use behavioural game theory to study LLMs' cooperation and coordination behaviour. Here we let different LLMs play finitely repeated 2 × 2 games with each other, with human-like strategies, and actual human players. Our results show that LLMs perform particularly well at self-interested games such as the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma family. However, they behave suboptimally in games that require coordination, such as the Battle of the Sexes. We verify that these behavioural signatures are stable across robustness checks. We also show how GPT-4's behaviour can be modulated by providing additional information about its opponent and by using a 'social chain-of-thought' strategy. This also leads to better scores and more successful coordination when interacting with human players. These results enrich our understanding of LLMs' social behaviour and pave the way for a behavioural game theory for machines. topics.summary: Human hunter-gatherer groups were commonly thought to be broadly egalitarian, with increasingly formal hierarchical social structures hypothesized to spread following the introduction of agriculture. topics.summary: The rapid expansion of residential areas in cities’ surroundings is drastically changing the character of rural landscapes. This spread of low-density, discontinuous urban development brings with it important social and environmental challenges. Despite these issues, people continue to migrate to these often-named peri-urban areas, even though the migration of large numbers of people irreversibly transforms the very qualities that initially drew them into these spaces. topics.topic: Sleepiness, Not Lost Sleep, Triggers Seizures
topics.summary: Sleep loss has been associated with increased seizure risk since antiquity. Using automated video detection of spontaneous seizures in Drosophila epilepsy models, we show that seizures worsen only when sleep restriction raises homeostatic "sleep drive," not simply when total sleep amount falls. This is supported by the paradoxical finding that acute activation of sleep-promoting circuits worsens seizures, because it increases sleep drive without changing sleep amount. Sleep-promoting circuits become hyperactive after sleep loss and are associated with increased whole-brain activity. During sleep restriction, optogenetic inhibition of sleep-promoting circuits to reduce sleep drive protects against seizures. Downregulation of the 5HT1A serotonin receptor in sleep-promoting cells mediates the effect of sleep drive on seizures, and we identify an FDA-approved 5HT1A agonist to mitigate seizures. Our findings demonstrate that while homeostatic sleep is needed to recoup lost sleep, sleep drive comes at the cost of increasing seizure susceptibility. topics.summary: Animals are not known to biosynthesize floral signals to manipulate pollinators, although such mimicry could profoundly shape plant-pollinator interactions. Larvae of the poisonous European blister beetle Meloe proscarabaeus parasitize multiple solitary bee species, yet the mechanism enabling host attraction has remained unresolved. Chemical analyses reveal a complex blend of monoterpenoids derived from ( S )-linalool, a ubiquitous floral volatile. Behavioral assays demonstrate that these compounds function as floral cues, eliciting attraction in bees. topics.summary: Humans emitted millions of tons of the toxic element lead (Pb) into the atmosphere. Here, we show that the Arctic Ocean received a dPb flux of 611 ± 74 Mg·a -1 from the North Atlantic Ocean in 2015/2016, making the Arctic Ocean a previously unrecognized net sink of Atlantic dPb (378 ± 85 Mg·a -1 ). This input is comparable to Arctic riverine dPb discharge (344 ± 222 Mg·a -1 ). Elevated dPb concentrations in the North Atlantic Ocean prior to the global-phase out of leaded gasoline (1986-2021) suggests ~5-fold higher fluxes from the North Atlantic in the late 1980s relative to 2015/2016, explaining the widespread contamination of Arctic abyssal sediments with Pb. topics.summary: Lake heatwaves (extreme hot water events) can substantially disrupt aquatic ecosystems. Here we analyse the characteristics of subsurface lake heatwaves (extreme hot events occurring below the surface) using a spatiotemporal modelling framework. Our findings reveal that subsurface heatwaves are frequent, often longer lasting but less intense than surface events. Deep-water heatwaves (bottom heatwaves) have increased in frequency (7.2 days decade −1 ), duration (2.1 days decade −1 ) and intensity (0.2 °C days decade −1 ) over the past 40 years. By the end of the century, changes in heatwave patterns, particularly under high emissions, are projected to intensify. topics.summary: Extreme event attribution assesses how anthropogenic climate change affected an extreme climate event, but typically focuses on individual events. Here, we systematize this approach, and apply it to 187 historical heatwaves reported over the period 2000-2022. We show that climate change has made all these heatwaves more likely and more intense. In particular, 33% of these heatwaves were virtually impossible without anthropogenic influence. Furthermore, this influence rises over time, both in intensity and in likelihood: climate change made the median heatwaves 24 times more likely over 2000-2009, 293 times more likely over 2010-2019 and 1355 times more likely over 2020-2022. We also extend the attribution to the contribution of emitters, by quantifying how much these heatwaves were affected by the emissions of 122 carbon majors (fossil fuel and cement producers), assessed through their full value chain. topics.summary: Small planetary bodies record the processes that shaped the Solar System, but their surfaces and interiors often evolve in unexpected ways. Deimos, the potato-shaped, 12-km-diameter outer satellite of Mars, has a strikingly smooth surface covered by fine regolith, in contrast to its heavily cratered and grooved sibling, 22-km-diameter Phobos. topics.summary: Silicon solar cell costs are reducing dramatically with these cells now providing the majority of new electricity generation capacity worldwide. Cost reduction has been via economies of scale and steadily increasing sunlight energy conversion efficiency. The best experimental cells at 27.4% efficiency approach the 29.4% figure almost universally regarded as the limit on silicon cell performance. Here we show that assumptions in deducing this limit are too restrictive, since failing to incorporate sunlight directionality. Furthermore, we show how this directionality and the cell’s angular response can be quantified compatibly, using projections of angular dependencies of both onto the solar module plane. Even simple schemes for exploiting directionality, including installing solar modules facing the equator at near-latitude tilt, increase theoretical limiting efficiency above 29.4%. Highest gains are for cells designed for sunlight tracking systems, including common 1-axis trackers, with such cells having theoretical efficiency limits > 30%. In this work, we provide a strategy for ongoing improvements in commercial cell efficiency over this decade, additionally lowering cost via reduced cell thickness.... topics.summary: Accelerating energy transition towards renewables is central to net-zero emissions. However, building a global power system dominated by solar and wind energy presents immense challenges. Here, we demonstrate the potential of a globally interconnected solar-wind system to meet future electricity demands. We estimate that such a system could generate ~3.1 times the projected 2050 global electricity demand. By optimizing solar-wind deployment, storage capacity, and trans-regional transmission, the solar-wind penetration could be achieved using only 29.4% of the highest potential, with a 15.6% reduction in initial investment compared to a strategy without interconnection. Global interconnection improves energy efficiency, mitigates the variability of renewable energy, promotes energy availability, and eases the economic burden of decarbonization. Importantly, this interconnected system shows remarkable resilience to climate extremes, generation outages, transmission disruptions, and geopolitical conflicts. Our findings underscore the potential of global interconnection in enabling high renewable penetration and guiding sustainable energy transitions. In our study of China’s 100 most congested cities, big-data empowered adaptive traffic signals reduced peak-hour trip times by 11% and off-peak by 8%, yielding an estimated annual CO₂ reduction of 31.73 million tonnes. Widespread adoption will require enhanced data collection and processing systems, underscoring the need for policy and technological development. Our findings highlight the transformative potential of big-data-driven adaptive systems to alleviate congestion and promote urban sustainability. Backtracking links these icebergs to the main outlet glaciers in northeast Greenland and the Russian High Arctic. In northeast Greenland, the timing of glacier destabilization coincides with this rise, whereas sparse satellite coverage in the Russian sector limits temporal attribution despite indications of enhanced glacier activity. A model sensitivity study shows that, apart from intensified calving, a more dynamic sea ice cover enhances downstream transport of glacial ice. Along these pathways, increased iceberg activity could reshape deep-sea habitats through enhanced melt and associated lithogenic input, and elevate navigational hazards as maritime traffic expands in the Arctic. topics.category: Atomic and Molecular Physics, and Optics
topics.summary: Photon-recoil-based actuation enables maneuvering of micro- and nanoscale objects without beam steering or tight focusing, mitigating system complexity and photodamage. Recent light-driven microdrones achieved full control in two dimensions using multiple laser fields; however, for many applications, sacrificing degrees of freedom allows substantial miniaturization and improved propulsion efficiency. Here, we demonstrate sub-micrometer nanorobots actuated by a plasmonic directional antenna that simultaneously provides propulsion force and orientation control. The nanorobots reach propulsion speeds up to 50 μm/s, with their motion direction intrinsically locked perpendicular to the linear polarization axis. Circularly polarized light pulses lift the resulting twofold orientational degeneracy through spin-momentum transfer. Using opto-thermophoretic forces, nanorobots efficiently capture, transport, reversibly assemble, and release bacteria. By sequencing linear and circular polarization states, they execute complex, high-precision trajectories to systematically sweep defined regions, functioning as light-driven robotic cleaners. This work expands the capabilities of nanorobots for biological manipulation and high-speed, localized sensing. Topics: nanorobots, light propulsion, plasmonics, microrobots, bacteria manipulation, optics.

topics.topic: Robot Swarms With a Nervous System
topics.summary: We present the self-organizing nervous system (SoNS), a robot swarm architecture based on self-organized hierarchy. The SoNS approach enables robots to autonomously establish, maintain, and reconfigure dynamic multilevel system architectures. For example, a robot swarm consisting of n independent robots could transform into a single n –robot SoNS and then into several independent smaller SoNSs, where each SoNS uses a temporary and dynamic hierarchy. Leveraging the SoNS approach, we showed that sensing, actuation, and decision-making can be coordinated in a locally centralized way without sacrificing the benefits of scalability, flexibility, and fault tolerance, for which swarm robotics is usually studied. In several proof-of-concept robot missions—including binary decision-making and search and rescue—we demonstrated that the capabilities of the SoNS approach greatly advance the state of the art in swarm robotics. The missions were conducted with a real heterogeneous aerial-ground robot swarm, using a custom-developed quadrotor platform. We also demonstrated the scalability of the SoNS approach in swarms of up to 250 robots in a physics-based simulator and demonstrated several types of... Topics: swarm robotics, self-organization, drones, multi-robot systems, fault tolerance, search and rescue.

topics.topic: Robot Boats Made of Fish Food
topics.summary: Centimeter-scale aquatic robots could be used in environmental monitoring, exploration, and intervention in aquatic environments. However, existing robots rely on artificial polymers and commercial electronic components, which can pollute and disrupt sensitive ecological environments if they are not retrieved. To address these challenges, we describe a fully biodegradable and fully edible self-propelled device that leverages the Marangoni effect for autonomous propulsion. The body of the edible aquatic robot is made of freeze-dried fish food and is powered by a water-triggered pneumatic reaction that produces motion by sustained release of a surfactant that is safe for aquatic fauna. The device’s biodegradable and non-toxic composition allows for safe environmental deployment for environmental sensing, delivery of nutrition or medication in aquatic environments. The proposed method substantially expands the potential benefits of small-scale aquatic robots that could be deployed on a large scale without the need to retrieve them and even provide nutrition to wildlife at the end of their lifetime as animals do. topics.summary: Are large language models (LLMs) biased in favor of communications produced by LLMs, leading to possible antihuman discrimination? Using a classical experimental design inspired by employment discrimination studies, we tested widely used LLMs, including GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and a selection of recent open-weight models in binary choice scenarios. These involved LLM-based assistants selecting between goods (the goods we study include consumer products, academic papers, and film-viewings) described either by humans or LLMs. Our results show a consistent tendency for LLM-based AIs to prefer LLM-presented options. This suggests the possibility of future AI systems implicitly discriminating against humans as a class, giving AI agents and AI-assisted humans an unfair advantage. Topics: AI bias, large language models, GPT-4, discrimination, AI agents, experimental economics.

topics.summary: The adoption of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare demands a careful analysis of their potential to spread false medical knowledge. Because LLMs ingest massive volumes of data from the open Internet during training, they are potentially exposed to unverified medical knowledge that may include deliberately planted misinformation. Here, we perform a threat assessment that simulates a data-poisoning attack against The Pile, a popular dataset used for LLM development. We find that replacement of just 0.001% of training tokens with medical misinformation results in harmful models more likely to propagate medical errors. Furthermore, we discover that corrupted models match the performance of their corruption-free counterparts on open-source benchmarks routinely used to evaluate medical LLMs. Using biomedical knowledge graphs to screen medical LLM outputs, we propose a harm mitigation strategy that captures 91.9% of harmful content (F1 = 85.7%). Our algorithm provides a unique method to validate stochastically generated LLM outputs against hard-coded relationships in knowledge graphs. In view of current calls for improved data provenance and transparent LLM development, we... Topics: large language models, data poisoning, medical misinformation, AI safety, healthcare AI.

topics.topic: Longer AI Answers Seem More Right
topics.summary: As artificial intelligence systems, particularly large language models (LLMs), become increasingly integrated into decision-making processes, the ability to trust their outputs is crucial. To earn human trust, LLMs must be well calibrated such that they can accurately assess and communicate the likelihood of their predictions being correct. Whereas recent work has focused on LLMs’ internal confidence, less is understood about how effectively they convey uncertainty to users. Here we explore the calibration gap, which refers to the difference between human confidence in LLM-generated answers and the models’ actual confidence, and the discrimination gap, which reflects how well humans and models can distinguish between correct and incorrect answers. Our experiments with multiple-choice and short-answer questions reveal that users tend to overestimate the accuracy of LLM responses when provided with default explanations. Moreover, longer explanations increased user confidence, even when the extra length did not improve answer accuracy. By adjusting LLM explanations to better reflect the models’ internal confidence, both the calibration gap and the discrimination gap narrowed, significantly improving user perception... Topics: large language models, trust, calibration, uncertainty, human-AI interaction, explanations.

topics.topic: AI Predicts Lab Results Better Than Scientists
topics.summary: Scientific discoveries often hinge on synthesizing decades of research, a task that potentially outstrips human information processing capacities. Large language models (LLMs) offer a solution. LLMs trained on the vast scientific literature could potentially integrate noisy yet interrelated findings to forecast novel results better than human experts. Here, to evaluate this possibility, we created BrainBench, a forward-looking benchmark for predicting neuroscience results. We find that LLMs surpass experts in predicting experimental outcomes. BrainGPT, an LLM we tuned on the neuroscience literature, performed better yet. Like human experts, when LLMs indicated high confidence in their predictions, their responses were more likely to be correct, which presages a future where LLMs assist humans in making discoveries. Our approach is not neuroscience specific and is transferable to other knowledge-intensive endeavours. Topics: large language models, neuroscience, scientific prediction, BrainBench, AI in science.

topics.topic: Steering a Drone With a Tail Twist
topics.summary: A banked turn is a common flight maneuver observed in birds and aircraft. To initiate the turn, whereas traditional aircraft rely on the wing ailerons, most birds use a variety of asymmetric wing-morphing control techniques to roll their bodies and thus redirect the lift vector to the direction of the turn. Nevertheless, when searching for prey, soaring raptors execute steady banked turns without exhibiting observable wing movements apart from the tail twisting around the body axis. Although tail twisting can compensate for adverse yaw, functioning similarly to the vertical tail in aircraft, how raptors use only tail twisting to perform banked turns is still not well understood. Here, we developed and used a raptor-inspired feathered drone to find that the proximity of the tail to the wings causes asymmetric wing-induced flows over the twisted tail and thus lift asymmetry, resulting in both roll and yaw moments sufficient to coordinate banked turns. topics.summary: Identifying the mechanisms that underlie cooperation is fundamental to biology 1 . The most complex form of cooperation in vertebrates occurs in cooperative breeders, in which helpers forego reproduction and assist in raising the young of others, typically relatives 2 . Not all cooperative societies, however, are kin-based—nearly half of all avian 3 and mammalian 4 cooperative breeders form mixed-kin societies, much like those of humans 5 . Kin selection in mixed-kin societies occurs when individuals gain indirect fitness from the preferential helping of relatives 6 , but helpers also frequently assist non-kin 7 , highlighting a potential role for direct fitness in stabilizing cooperative societies 7,8 . Here, using a 20-year study of superb starlings ( Lamprotornis superbus ), we examined how direct and indirect fitness jointly influence helping behaviour. Although we detected kin-biased helping (demonstrating kin selection), non-kin helping was common despite opportunities to aid kin. topics.topic: Radar Counts Birds at Risk From Turbines

source.institution: University of Amsterdam, Netherlands & Cornell University, USA

topics.summary: With global ambitions to decarbonize the energy system, wind power capacity will continue to increase dramatically worldwide. This raises concerns about environmental impacts of wind energy infrastructure and operations, particularly for collision of aerial wildlife. Using a network of weather surveillance radars, we quantified numbers, timing and spatial extent of nightly and annual large-scale bird movements over Western Europe. We also mapped onshore wind turbines and calculated potential energy production using wind speed and distribution data. Integrating bird movement patterns, turbine characteristics and energy production, we estimated the number of birds that are potentially at risk of collision because they fly in proximity to wind turbines and at heights of rotating blades. To demonstrate potential for designing measures to mitigate risk to aerial biodiversity, we derive curtailment scenarios and compare costs and benefits for energy production and conserving biodiversity and show that surprisingly efficient trade-offs may be possible. topics.summary: As the body’s primary source of energy, the maintenance of blood glucose is indispensable for overall health and metabolic homeostasis. topics.topic: Heart Muscle Patches From Stem Cells
topics.summary: Cardiomyocytes can be implanted to remuscularize the failing heart 1–7 . topics.topic: Running Doesn't Rev Up Monkey Vision

source.institution: University of Texas at Austin, USA

topics.summary: When mice run, activity in their primary visual cortex (V1) is strongly modulated. This observation has altered conceptions of a brain region assumed to be a passive image processor. Extensive work has followed to dissect the circuits and functions of running-correlated modulation. However, it remains unclear whether visual processing in primates might similarly change during locomotion. We therefore measured V1 activity in marmosets while they viewed stimuli on a treadmill. In contrast to mouse, running-correlated modulations of marmoset V1 were small and tended to be slightly suppressive. Population-level analyses revealed trial-to-trial fluctuations of shared gain across V1 in both species, but while strongly correlated with running in mice, gain modulations were smaller and more often negatively correlated with running in marmosets. Thus, population-wide fluctuations of V1 may reflect a common feature of mammalian visual cortical function, but important quantitative differences point to distinct consequences for the relation between vision and action in primates versus rodents. Topics: visual cortex, locomotion, marmosets, mice, neuroscience, primates.

topics.summary: Tympanal organs as "insect ears" have evolved repeatedly. Dinidorid stinkbugs were reported to possess a conspicuous tympanal organ on female's hindlegs. Here we report an unexpected discovery that the stinkbug's "tympanal organ" is actually a novel symbiotic organ. The stinkbug's "tympanum" is not membranous but a porous cuticle, where each pore connects to glandular secretory cells. In reproductive females, the hindleg organ is covered with fungal hyphae growing out of the pores. Upon oviposition, the females skillfully transfer the fungi from the organ to the eggs. The eggs are quickly covered with hyphae and physically protected against wasp parasitism. The fungi are mostly benign Cordycipitaceae entomopathogens and show considerable diversity among insect individuals and populations, indicating environmental acquisition of specific fungal associates. These results uncover a novel external fungal symbiosis in which host's elaborate morphological, physiological and behavioral specializations underpin the selective recruitment of benign entomopathogens for a defensive purpose. Topics: stinkbugs, symbiosis, fungi, parasitic wasps, insect anatomy, entomology.

topics.summary: Natural selection has repeatedly led to the evolution of two alternative antipredator color strategies-camouflage to avoid detection and aposematism to advertise unprofitability-but we lack understanding of how ecological context favors one strategy over the other. We conducted a globally replicated predation experiment at 21 sites on six continents to test how predator community, prey community, and visual environment influenced the predation risk of 15,018 artificial paper "moth" prey with cryptic or warning coloration. Results indicated that aposematic strategies fare better in environments with low predation intensity, whereas camouflage strategies are advantaged when other camouflaged prey species are rare and when light levels are low. This study demonstrates how multiple mechanisms shape antipredator strategies, helping to explain the evolution and global distribution of camouflaged and aposematic animals. topics.topic: Shifting Winds Trap a Rice Pest

source.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

topics.summary: Many insect migrants rely on favorable seasonal winds to carry out long-range latitudinal migrations. In East China, the annual advance and retreat of the East Asian summer monsoon produces ideal conditions for seasonal range expansion and contraction of many migratory crop pests. However, climate-induced changes in the strength, timing, and location of the monsoon are impacting wind systems which may, in turn, affect migration patterns. We investigated these questions in the rice leafroller (RLR) moth, a severe pest of rice that annually invades the Lower Yangtze River Valley (LYRV) of China from winter-breeding areas further south. Using a 24-y dataset of RLR population dynamics from 31 monitoring stations across Southeast China, we investigated the impact of changes in monsoon wind regimes on fall migration patterns of the pest. Historically, RLR emigrated from the LYRV to South China on the favorably directed winds produced by the retreat of the monsoon at the end of the outbreak season (from mid-August onward). topics.summary: Our algorithmic understanding of vision has been revolutionized by a reverse engineering paradigm that involves building artificial systems that perform the same tasks as biological systems. Here, we extend this paradigm to social behavior. We embodied artificial neural networks in artificial fish and raised the artificial fish in virtual fish tanks that mimicked the rearing conditions of biological fish. When artificial fish had deep reinforcement learning and curiosity-derived rewards, they spontaneously developed fish-like social behaviors, including collective behavior and social preferences (favoring in-group over out-group members). The artificial fish also developed social behavior in naturalistic ocean worlds, showing that these embodied models generalize to real-world learning contexts. Thus, animal-like social behaviors can develop from generic learning algorithms (reinforcement learning and intrinsic motivation). Our study provides a foundation for reverse-engineering the development of social behavior using image-computable models from artificial intelligence, bridging the divide between high-dimensional sensory inputs and collective action. Topics: artificial intelligence, collective behavior, fish schooling, reinforcement learning, curiosity, development.

topics.summary: Understanding the spawning strategies of large pelagic fish could provide insights into their underlying evolutionary drivers, but large-scale information on spawning remains limited. Here we leverage a near-global larval dataset of 15 large pelagic fish taxa to develop habitat suitability models and use these as a proxy for spawning grounds. Our analysis reveals considerable consistency in spawning in time and space, with 10 taxa spawning in spring/summer and 9 taxa spawning off Northwest Australia. Considering the vast ocean expanse available for spawning, these results suggest that the evolutionary benefits of co-locating spawning in terms of advantageous larval conditions outweigh the benefits of segregated spawning in terms of reduced competition and lower larval predation. Further, tropical species spawn over broad areas throughout the year, whereas more subtropical and temperate species spawn in more restricted areas and seasons. These insights into the spawning strategies of large pelagic fish could inform marine management, including through fisheries measures to protect spawners and through the placement of marine protected areas. topics.summary: We urgently need to restore degraded tropical forests to mitigate the climate and biodiversity crises, but how to do so rapidly and cost-effectively remains an open question. Here, we provide a long-term, landscape-scale assessment of the effectiveness of enrichment tree planting and liana cutting, the two most common restoration interventions used across many tropical regions. Leveraging one of the world's largest and longest-running forest restoration experiments, we used repeated airborne laser scanning to track the 3D structural recovery of 500 ha of once-logged rainforest in Borneo. Over an 18-year period, enrichment planting increased mean canopy height by 1.6 m relative to unplanted controls. Remarkably, liana cutting increased canopy height more than four times faster (3.7 m over just 9 years). This recovery was jointly driven by accelerated tree growth and a 50% reduction in tree mortality. Given that liana cutting is around 10 times cheaper to implement than enrichment planting, our results suggest it provides a cost-effective, scalable solution to accelerate the structural recovery of logged tropical forests. Topics: forest restoration, lianas, tropical rainforest, Borneo, logging, lidar, tree planting.

topics.summary: Trees are an important carbon sink as they accumulate biomass through photosynthesis1. Identifying tree species that grow fast is therefore commonly considered to be essential for effective climate change mitigation through forest planting. Although species characteristics are key information for plantation design and forest management, field studies often fail to detect clear relationships between species functional traits and tree growth2. Here, by consolidating four independent datasets and classifying the acquisitive and conservative species based on their functional trait values, we show that acquisitive tree species, which are supposedly fast-growing species, generally grow slowly in field conditions. This discrepancy between the current paradigm and field observations is explained by the interactions with environmental conditions that influence growth. Acquisitive species require moist mild climates and fertile soils, conditions that are generally not met in the field. By contrast, conservative species, which are supposedly slow-growing species, show generally higher realized growth due to their ability to tolerate unfavourable environmental conditions. In general, conservative tree species grow more steadily than acquisitive tree species in... Topics: tree growth, functional traits, forest planting, carbon sink, ecology, forestry.

topics.summary: Trees can differ enormously in their crown architectural traits, such as the scaling relationships between tree height, crown width and stem diameter. Yet despite the importance of crown architecture in shaping the structure and function of terrestrial ecosystems, we lack a complete picture of what drives this incredible diversity in crown shapes. Using data from 374,888 globally distributed trees, we explore how climate, disturbance, competition, functional traits, and evolutionary history constrain the height and crown width scaling relationships of 1914 tree species. We find that variation in height-diameter scaling relationships is primarily controlled by water availability and light competition. Conversely, crown width is predominantly shaped by exposure to wind and fire, while also covarying with functional traits related to mechanical stability and photosynthesis. Additionally, we identify several plant lineages with highly distinctive stem and crown forms, such as the exceedingly slender dipterocarps of Southeast Asia, or the extremely wide crowns of legume trees in African savannas. Our study charts the global spectrum of tree crown architecture and pinpoints the processes... Topics: tree architecture, crown shape, forests, savannas, climate, wind, fire, ecology.

truth.text: Measurements of nearly 375,000 trees of 1,914 species worldwide show water and competition for light set how tall trees grow for their trunk width, while wind and fire mostly set how wide their crowns spread.
facts: Crown architecture is the 3D shape of a tree's branches and leaves
Trees in dense forests race upward toward light
Fire and strong winds favor sturdier, differently shaped crowns
Southeast Asia's dipterocarps are exceptionally slender and tall
African savanna legume trees, like acacias, have exceptionally wide crowns

source.institution: University of the Witwatersrand, South Africa & Stanford University, USA

topics.summary: Population studies provide insights into the interplay between the gut microbiome and geographical, lifestyle, genetic and environmental factors. However, low- and middle-income countries, in which approximately 84% of the world’s population lives1, are not equitably represented in large-scale gut microbiome research2–4. Here we present the AWI-Gen 2 Microbiome Project, a cross-sectional gut microbiome study sampling 1,801 women from Burkina Faso, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa. By engaging with communities that range from rural and horticultural to post-industrial and urban informal settlements, we capture a far greater breadth of the world’s population diversity. Using shotgun metagenomic sequencing, we identify taxa with geographic and lifestyle associations, including Treponema and Cryptobacteroides species loss and Bifidobacterium species gain in urban populations. We uncover 1,005 bacterial metagenome-assembled genomes, and we identify antibiotic susceptibility as a factor that might drive Treponema succinifaciens absence in urban populations. Finally, we find an HIV infection signature defined by several taxa not previously associated with HIV, including Dysosmobacter welbionis and Enterocloster sp. This study represents the largest population-representative survey of... Topics: gut microbiome, Africa, urbanization, antibiotics, metagenomics, HIV, women's health.

truth.text: Gut microbes of 1,801 women in Burkina Faso, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa revealed 1,005 bacterial genomes, and city-dwellers had lost some bacteria common in rural women, likely partly through antibiotics.
facts: The gut microbiome is the community of microbes living in our intestines
About 84% of people live in low- and middle-income countries, rarely studied
Women ranged from rural farmers to residents of urban informal settlements
Urban women gained other bacteria, like Bifidobacterium, used in probiotics
The study also found a gut signature linked to HIV infection

topics.summary: Understanding the factors that shape variation in the human microbiome is a major goal of research in biology. While other genomics fields have used large, pre-compiled compendia to extract systematic insights requiring otherwise impractical sample sizes, there has been no comparable resource for the 16S rRNA sequencing data commonly used to quantify microbiome composition. To help close this gap, we have assembled a set of 168,484 publicly available human gut microbiome samples, processed with a single pipeline and combined into the largest unified microbiome dataset to date. We use this resource, which is freely available at microbiomap.org, to shed light on global variation in the human gut microbiome. We find that Firmicutes, particularly Bacilli and Clostridia, are almost universally present in the human gut. At the same time, the relative abundance of the 65 most common microbial genera differ between at least two world regions. We also show that gut microbiomes in undersampled world regions, such as Central and Southern Asia, differ significantly from the more thoroughly characterized microbiomes of... Topics: gut microbiome, global health, bacteria, big data, Asia, microbiome research.

truth.text: Combining 168,000 public gut microbiome samples into one dataset showed that gut microbes in neglected regions like Central and South Asia differ markedly from the well-studied microbiomes of Europe and North America.

topics.topic: The Hidden Factor in Gut Studies
topics.summary: The microbiota in individual habitats differ in both relative composition and absolute abundance. While sequencing approaches determine the relative abundances of taxa and genes, they do not provide information on their absolute abundances. Here, we developed a machine-learning approach to predict fecal microbial loads (microbial cells per gram) solely from relative abundance data. Applying our prediction model to a large-scale metagenomic dataset (n = 34,539), we demonstrated that microbial load is the major determinant of gut microbiome variation and is associated with numerous host factors, including age, diet, and medication. We further found that for several diseases, changes in microbial load, rather than the disease condition itself, more strongly explained alterations in patients' gut microbiome. Adjusting for this effect substantially reduced the statistical significance of the majority of disease-associated species. Our analysis reveals that the fecal microbial load is a major confounder in microbiome studies, highlighting its importance for understanding microbiome variation in health and disease. Topics: gut microbiome, microbial load, confounding, metagenomics, disease associations, machine learning.

truth.text: How many microbes are in a gram of stool, not which kinds, turned out to be the biggest driver of differences in gut microbiomes across 34,500 people, and it explained away many reported links between microbes and diseases.
facts: Most microbiome studies measure only proportions of each microbe, not totals
A machine-learning model estimated total microbial load from proportions
Load varied with age, diet and medications
After adjusting for load, most disease-linked species lost significance
So many "disease microbes" may just reflect fewer or more microbes overall

topics.topic: Babies Swap Gut Microbes at Daycare
topics.summary: The early infant microbiome is largely primed by microbial transmission from the mother between birth and the first few weeks of life1–3, but how interpersonal transmission further shapes the developing microbiome in the first year remains unexplored. Here we report a metagenomic survey to model microbiome transmission in the nursery setting among babies attending the first year, their educators and their families (n = 134 individuals). We performed dense longitudinal microbiome sampling (n = 1,013 faecal samples) during the first year of nursery and tracked microbial strain transmission within and between nursery groups across 3 different facilities. We detected extensive baby-to-baby microbiome transmission within nursery groups even after only 1 month of nursery attendance, with nursery-acquired strains accounting for a proportion of the infant gut microbiome comparable to that from family by the end of the first term. Baby-to-baby transmission continued to grow over the nursery year, in an increasingly intricate transmission network with single strains spreading in some classes, and with multiple baby-acquisition and species-transmissibility patterns. Having siblings was... Topics: infant gut microbiome, daycare, microbial transmission, nursery, child health, metagenomics.

Researchers analyzed over 1,000 stool samples from babies, teachers and families
Strain-level DNA tracking shows exactly who shared which bacteria
Sharing was detectable after just one month at nursery
